title: Book I: Miss Brooke — Chapter IV
paragraphs: 1st Gentleman. Our actions are the chains we forge for ourselves.
2nd Gentleman. Yes, that's true; but I think the world supplies the iron.
“Sir James seems determined to do whatever you want,” Celia said as they drove home after inspecting the new building site.
“He's a good soul, and more sensible than anyone would expect,” Dorothea answered without thinking.
“You mean he seems rather foolish.”
“No, no,” Dorothea said, checking herself and briefly resting her hand on her sister's. “But he doesn't speak equally well about every subject.”
“I should think only disagreeable people do that,” Celia replied in her usual purring tone. “They must be dreadful to live with. Just imagine! At breakfast, and all the time.”

Dorothea laughed. “Oh, Kitty, what a wonderful creature you are!” She pinched Celia's chin, now inclined to find her irresistibly lovely and charming, fitted to become an everlasting cherub, and, if doctrine allowed one to say it, scarcely more in need of salvation than a squirrel. “Of course people needn't always talk well. It's only that you can judge the quality of their minds when they try to.”
“You mean Sir James makes the attempt and fails.”
“I was making a general remark. Why are you interrogating me about Sir James? Pleasing me isn't the purpose of his life.”
“Really, Dodo, can you honestly believe that?”

“Certainly. He sees me as a future sister, nothing more.” Dorothea had never hinted at this before. A shyness about such matters, shared by both sisters, had made her wait for some decisive event to introduce it. Celia blushed, but immediately replied—

“Please stop making that mistake, Dodo. When Tantripp brushed my hair the other day, she told me Sir James's servant had heard from Mrs. Cadwallader's maid that Sir James was going to marry the older Miss Brooke.”

“How can you let Tantripp gossip like that to you, Celia?” Dorothea said indignantly. She was no less angry because details asleep in her memory were waking up to confirm this unwelcome discovery. “You must have questioned her. It's degrading.”

“I see no harm whatever in Tantripp talking to me. It's better to hear what people are saying. You see the mistakes you make by getting ideas into your head. I'm perfectly sure Sir James intends to propose, and he thinks you'll accept him, especially since you've been so pleased with him over the plans. And uncle too—I know he expects it. Anyone can see Sir James is very much in love with you.”

The reversal in Dorothea's mind was so violent and painful that tears welled up and poured down. Every cherished plan turned bitter. She was disgusted to imagine Sir James believing she acknowledged him as her lover. She was distressed on Celia's account as well.
“How could he expect that?” she burst out with her greatest vehemence. “I've never agreed with him about anything except the cottages. Before that I was scarcely even polite.”
“But you've been so pleased with him ever since. He's begun to feel quite certain you're fond of him.”
“Fond of him, Celia! How can you use such a hateful expression?” Dorothea demanded passionately.
“Goodness, Dorothea, I imagine being fond of a man would be proper enough if you accepted him as your husband.”
“It offends me to hear that Sir James could suppose I was fond of him. Besides, that isn't the right word for what I would need to feel towards a man I agreed to marry.”

“Well, I'm sorry for Sir James. I thought I ought to tell you, because you were carrying on as usual, never looking where you are and stepping in the wrong place. You always see things nobody else sees, and it's impossible to satisfy you; yet you never notice what's perfectly plain. That's your way, Dodo.” Something had certainly lent Celia unusual courage. She was not sparing the sister she sometimes held in awe. Who knows what fair criticisms Murr the Cat may be making of us creatures with our wider speculations?

“It's very painful,” Dorothea said, feeling whipped. “I can't have anything more to do with the cottages. I must be rude to him. I must tell him I want no part in them. It's very painful.” Tears filled her eyes again.

“Wait a little and think it over. You know he's going away for a day or two to visit his sister. There'll only be Lovegood.” Celia could not help softening. “Poor Dodo,” she continued in kindly clipped phrases. “It is hard. Drawing plans is your favourite _fad_.”

“A _fad_ for drawing plans! Do you think I care about my fellow creatures' homes in that childish way? No wonder I make mistakes. How can anyone ever do anything nobly Christian among people whose thoughts are so petty?”

They said no more. Dorothea was too shaken to recover her composure and behave in a way that admitted any fault of her own. She preferred to blame the intolerable narrowness and half-blind conscience of the society around her. Celia was no longer an eternal cherub but a thorn in her spirit, a pink-and-white unbeliever, worse than any discouraging figure in “Pilgrim's Progress.” The _fad_ for drawing plans! What was life worth, what great faith could exist, if the entire meaning of one's actions could shrivel into such dried-up rubbish? When she stepped out of the carriage her cheeks were pale and her eyelids red. She looked the picture of sorrow. Her uncle, meeting her in the hall, would have been alarmed if Celia had not stood beside her looking so pretty and calm that he immediately attributed Dorothea's tears to excessive religion. During their absence he had returned from the county town, where he had gone concerning a petition to pardon a criminal.
“Well, my dears,” he said kindly as they came to kiss him, “I hope nothing unpleasant has happened while I've been away.”
“No, uncle,” Celia answered. “We've been to Freshitt to see the cottages. We expected you home for lunch.”
“I stopped at Lowick for lunch—you didn't know I'd come through Lowick. And I've brought two pamphlets for you, Dorothea. In the library, you know; they're on the library table.”

An electric current seemed to pass through Dorothea, thrilling her out of despair into expectation. The pamphlets concerned the early Church. She shook off the oppression of Celia, Tantripp and Sir James and went straight to the library. Celia went upstairs. A message detained Mr. Brooke, but when he returned to the library he found Dorothea seated, already absorbed in a pamphlet with some notes by Mr. Casaubon in the margins. She took it in as eagerly as she might have breathed the fragrance of fresh flowers after a dry, hot, dreary walk.
She was escaping Tipton and Freshitt, and her own unhappy tendency to put her feet wrong on the road to the New Jerusalem.

Mr. Brooke settled in his armchair and stretched his legs towards the wood fire, now collapsed into a marvellous mass of glowing dice between the firedogs. Gently rubbing his hands, he looked mildly at Dorothea with an unhurried, neutral air, as though he had nothing particular to say. As soon as she noticed him, she closed her pamphlet and stood as if to leave. Usually she would have taken an interest in his errand of mercy for the criminal, but her recent distress had left her distracted.

“I came back by Lowick, you know,” Mr. Brooke said, apparently not to stop her leaving but from his usual inclination to repeat himself. This fundamental principle of human speech showed especially clearly in Mr. Brooke. “I lunched there and saw Casaubon's library and that sort of thing. The air's sharp when you're driving. Won't you sit down, my dear? You look cold.”

Dorothea was quite willing to accept. When her uncle's easy way of taking things did not happen to exasperate her, it could be soothing. She took off her bonnet and cloak and sat opposite him, enjoying the heat while raising her beautiful hands to shield her face. They were neither thin nor small, but strong, feminine, motherly hands. She seemed to hold them up in atonement for her passionate desire to know and think, which in the unfriendly atmosphere of Tipton and Freshitt had ended in tears and reddened eyelids.
Now she remembered the condemned prisoner. “What news have you brought about the sheep thief, uncle?”
“What, poor Bunch? Well, it seems we can't save him. He's to be hanged.”
Dorothea's brow registered both condemnation and pity.
“Hanged, you know,” Mr. Brooke repeated with a quiet nod. “Poor Romilly! He'd have helped us. I knew Romilly. Casaubon didn't. He's rather buried in his books, you know, Casaubon is.”
“When a man has great studies to pursue and a great work to write, of course he has to give up much social life. How can he go round making acquaintances?”

“True enough. But a man gets gloomy, you know. I've always been a bachelor myself, but my temperament kept me from moping. I used to go everywhere and take everything in. I never moped. But I can see Casaubon does, you know. He needs a companion—a companion, you know.”
“Being his companion would be a great honour for anyone,” Dorothea said with energy.

“You like him, do you?” Mr. Brooke said without surprise or any other visible emotion. “Well, I've known Casaubon ten years, ever since he came to Lowick. But I've never got anything out of him—ideas, you know. Still, he's a first-rate man and might become a bishop, that sort of thing, if Peel stays in office. And he thinks very highly of you, my dear.”
Dorothea found herself unable to speak.

“The fact is, his opinion of you is very high indeed. And he expresses himself remarkably well, Casaubon does. He's deferred to me because you haven't come of age. In short, I promised to speak to you, though I told him I thought his chances were small. I had to tell him that. My niece is very young, I said, and that kind of thing. But I didn't think I needed to go into everything. Anyway, the long and short of it is that he has asked my permission to propose marriage to you—marriage, you know,” Mr. Brooke said with his explanatory nod. “I thought I'd better tell you, my dear.”

Nothing in Mr. Brooke's manner betrayed anxiety, but he genuinely wanted to know his niece's thoughts so he could offer timely advice if needed. Whatever feeling he could find room for, as a magistrate who had absorbed so many ideas, was entirely kind. When Dorothea did not answer at once, he repeated, “I thought I'd better tell you, my dear.”
“Thank you, uncle,” Dorothea said clearly and steadily. “I'm deeply grateful to Mr. Casaubon. If he proposes, I'll accept him. I admire and respect him more than any man I've ever met.”

After a short pause Mr. Brooke said slowly, in a low voice, “Ah? … Well! In some ways he's a good match. But now, Chettam is a good match too, and our estates adjoin. I'll never oppose your wishes, my dear. People should have their own way in marriage and such things—up to a point, you know. I've always said that: up to a point. I want you to marry well, and I have good reason to think Chettam wants to marry you. I only mention it, you know.”
“I could never possibly marry Sir James Chettam,” Dorothea said. “If he has any thought of marrying me, he's badly mistaken.”
“That's just it, you see. You never can tell. I'd have thought Chettam exactly the sort of man a woman would like.”
“Please don't speak of him in that way again, uncle,” Dorothea said, feeling her earlier irritation return.

Mr. Brooke marvelled. Women, he felt, were an inexhaustible subject of study, since even at his age he could not predict them with scientific accuracy. Here was a fellow like Chettam without the slightest chance.

“Well, but Casaubon, now. There's no rush—not for you, I mean. Every year will make a difference to him, it's true. He's over forty-five, you know. A good twenty-seven years older than you, I'd say. Still, if it's learning and standing you like, and that sort of thing, we can't have everything. His income is good; he has a handsome estate apart from the Church. A good income. But he isn't young, and I mustn't hide from you, my dear, that I don't think his health is especially strong. I know nothing else against him.”
“I wouldn't want a husband very close to my own age,” Dorothea said with solemn conviction. “I'd want one whose judgment and knowledge were superior to mine in every way.”
Mr. Brooke repeated his quiet “Ah? I thought you had more opinions of your own than most girls. I thought you liked your own opinions—liked them, you know.”
“I can't imagine living without opinions, but I'd want sound reasons for them. A wise man could help me understand which opinions rested on the strongest foundations, and help me live by them.”

“Very true. You couldn't put it better—couldn't put it better beforehand, you know. But things turn out oddly,” Mr. Brooke continued, his conscience genuinely urging him to do his best for his niece. “Life isn't poured into a mould, isn't measured out by rule and line and that sort of thing. I never married, and you and yours will benefit from that. The truth is, I never loved anyone enough to put my head into a noose for them. It _is_ a noose, you know. Temper, for instance. There's temper to consider. And a husband likes to be master.”
“I know I must expect difficulties, uncle. Marriage brings higher duties. I've never thought of it simply as personal comfort,” said poor Dorothea.

“Well, you aren't fond of display, a grand household, balls, dinners and all that. I can see Casaubon's habits might suit you better than Chettam's. You shall do as you choose, my dear. I wouldn't obstruct Casaubon; I said that immediately. You never know how anything will turn out. Your tastes aren't the same as every young lady's, and a clergyman and scholar—perhaps a future bishop, that sort of thing—might suit you better than Chettam. Chettam's a good fellow, sound at heart, you know, but he doesn't take much interest in ideas. I did at his age. But Casaubon's eyes, now. I think he's damaged them a little with too much reading.”
“The more opportunity I had to help him, uncle, the happier I would be,” Dorothea said fervently.

“I see you've quite decided. Well, my dear, the truth is that I have a letter for you in my pocket.” Mr. Brooke handed it to her, but as she stood to leave he added, “There's no great hurry, my dear. Think it over, you know.”

After Dorothea left, he reflected that he had certainly spoken forcefully. He had set out the risks of marriage in a striking way, as duty required. But as for claiming to know better than young people—no uncle, however widely he had travelled in youth, however many new ideas he had absorbed or famous people now dead he had dined with, could claim to judge what marriage would suit a girl who preferred Casaubon to Chettam. In short, woman was a problem before which Mr. Brooke's mind went blank, and could therefore scarcely be less complicated than the rotations of an irregular solid.
